chapter_theme: Akananuru 221 to 240, from the மணிமிடைபவளம் section: half the poems are paalai partings and comforts in which the friend argues from memory, glory or the lover's body that the man will return, set among kurinji night-tryst poems pressing for marriage, two mullai homecomings, two marutham reproaches and two neythal meetings, with puram fame (Kazhar, Uranthai, Unur, Uthiyan Cheral's feast, Nalli) used repeatedly as a scale of comparison.

221.reading: The friend tells the girl that, since their people have begun the wedding rites with toddy and heaped sand, she has arranged for her to leave with the dark-bearded young man of the new spear, who will crown her hair with kadamba blossoms, along the hard forest track where a tiger that missed its elephant roars and the she-elephant bolts.
221.nuance: The poem never says whom the kin mean to marry her to; that the wedding is not to her lover is the colophon's reading (போக்குடன்பட), and it is what makes the friend's arrangement urgent. The kadamba spray the young man will pick for her hair is a small wedding of their own set against the kin's wedding at home.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகற்குப் போக்குடன்பட்ட தோழி, தலைமகட்குப் போக்குடன்படச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl is to leave home with her lover over the dry track, the parting of udanpokku

222.reading: With the hill lord listening, the friend says that since the sickness he caused is wasting her beauty she will speak out: let us go, along the river cold with many nights of thunder and rain, to win a fame like Maruthi's, who showed Aathi Manthi her lover taken by the Kaveri at the Kazhar festival and then went into the sea.
222.nuance: The friend borrows a known story of love and drowning to hint at a desperate act; aimed at the overhearing hero, the hint presses him to marry rather than keep coming by the flooded night path. The Maruthi part of the legend is told only here in this chapter; poem 236 uses the same story from Manthi's side.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the great hill of the hero's country and the night rain on his path

comparisons.tenor: the fame the friend hopes the two of them will win

223.reading: The friend tells the grieving girl not to fear that the man who could leave her will forget her: though he has crossed the long shadeless waterless track where wind-tossed flame-of-the-forest pods curved like a boar's tusk blaze like a fire-spouting elephant, how could he sleep forgetting the sleep he found in her garlanded hair?
223.nuance: The comfort rests on his memory of her hair, which he once gathered over her shoulders and decked with athiral and kuvalai; the friend argues from the body's habit, not from his promise.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளைத் தோழி வற்புறுத்தியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the shadeless, waterless long track he has crossed

comparisons.tenor: the long curved pods of the flame-of-the-forest
the wind-lifted mass of red murukku blossom

224.reading: The hero, his task done, tells his charioteer to drive on as the day ends, horses breathing hot as a smith's bellows and flecked with milk-white froth, the wheel cutting the sand with the sound of a housewife's quern, while he pictures his wife pushing back her bangles and looking again and again toward the gate, asking whether he is coming.
224.nuance: The two domestic similes, the smith's bellows and the quern turned by a housewife, bring the home into the journey before he reaches it; the wife he imagines speaks only one line, and it is a question.

colophon.thurai: வினைமுற்றிய தலைமகன் தேர்ப்பாகற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife waits at home for the returning husband, in the woodland after the heat has gone

comparisons.tenor: the white froth on the horses
the sound of the wheel in the sand

225.reading: The hero asks his heart whether, after being one with her today in love, innocence and gentle speech, they will lodge tomorrow in a rainless hamlet on the hard track, where wind through bee-bored bamboo sounds like a herdsman's flute and iruppai flowers drop like loosened pearls, thinking of her anguished look and her sulking.
225.nuance: Today and tomorrow (இன்றே, நாளை) frame the poem: the whole journey is imagined from inside the embrace. The music of the bamboo is the one soft thing on the track, and it belongs to the herders' land, not the desert.

colophon.thurai: பொருள் கடைக்கூட்டிய நெஞ்சிற்குத் தலைமகன் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hard track and the hamlet the rain has forgotten

comparisons.tenor: the wind sounding through the bored bamboo
the iruppai flowers falling on the red ground

226.reading: The friend refuses the lord of the rich town his tricks: his bathing yesterday in the Kaveri's dawn flood at Matthi's Kazhar ford with the woman he desires has raised more uproar than the shout when Katti fled without a fight on hearing the kinai drum at Thithan Veliyan's court in Uranthai.
226.nuance: The scale is the joke: a private bathe is measured against a famous rout, and the hero is mocked by being set beside a king who ran. The women scaring herons with sedge in the karanthai fields are the town's ordinary life, which has now seen him.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகற்குத் தோழி வாயின் மறுத்தது.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband's bathing with another woman, the sulking of the marutham house

227.reading: The friend tells the girl to stop brooding over her pale forehead and slack shoulders: though he has crossed many tracks where a lone tusker in musth tears at a vengai and roars like warriors taking a field, may our lover stay well, he who left with a clamour like the bright market of Marungur beyond Thazhumban's Unur.
227.nuance: The friend's blessing, நோய்இலராக, turns comfort into a wish for the absent man. Thazhumban is praised for a drum that brought Tamil under it (தமிழ் அகப்படுத்த), an early use of தமிழ் for a land or people; line 17's பிடிமிதி வழுதுணை is obscure to us.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகட்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது. பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the red-dust tracks the tusker roams

occasion.words: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகட்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது

228.reading: With the hero listening, the friend says it would be well enough if he spent the days with them bathing in the kuvalai pool under the cold slope, and went home at night; but on the moonlit path to his hamlet the vengai blossoms look like a tiger's spots and the she-elephant bolts.
228.nuance: The danger is an illusion of moonlight, yet the friend uses it to turn him from night meetings to day ones, and in the end toward marriage. The she-elephant fleeing a flowering tree it takes for a tiger is a traditional candidate for a hidden sense (the girl's fears for him); it does not pass the act condition here, so it stays scene.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the cold hill slope and the moonlit night

occasion.words: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தோழி சொல்லியது

229.reading: The girl answers her friend's comfort: you tell me not to grieve as tears blur my eyes and gold-like pallor spreads, yet he who crossed the far hills of a waterless track where starving she-elephants stand like huts of a deserted village, and promised to come at once, has not come even in the sweet young spring when the cuckoo calls from the mango.
229.nuance: The spring is the proof: the cuckoo's call marks the season by which he promised to be back, so the beauty of the season is itself the evidence against him. The poem gives his own words, இன்னே வருதும், only to set them against the calendar.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளை வற்புறுத்துந் தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் வன்புறை யெதிரழிந்து சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the waterless long track he crossed

occasion.words: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளை வற்புறுத்துந் தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் வன்புறை யெதிரழிந்து சொல்லியது

230.reading: The hero tells his heart how he asked the shore girl in her leaf skirt, gathering punnai pollen like gold with her playmates, whether any harm would come if the right of this house were joined to him, and how, as his chariot drew near, she held back her tears and bowed her head a little, leaving him in great pain.
230.nuance: Her answer is a gesture, not a word: the bowed head and checked tears can be read as consent or as refusal, and the hero's pain comes from not knowing which. His proposal is couched in the language of household right (மனைக் கிழமை), unusual in a first meeting.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகளைக் கண்ணுற்று நீங்கும் தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater, its neythal flowers and the punnai pollen on the sand

comparisons.tenor: the large flowers of her leaf skirt

occasion.words: தலைமகளைக் கண்ணுற்று நீங்கும் தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

231.reading: The friend tells the girl that men who prize fame, holding that crushing foes and helping kin in need are not for those who stay home, have crossed the dreaded track of hunters' victims under stone heaps, yet they will come back with melting hearts, those who lay in her bee-loud hair, which is like the Pandyan's famed Koodal.
231.nuance: The friend argues with a puram value: glory is earned away from home, so the parting is honourable, and the same honour guarantees the return. The stone heaps over men killed by forest bowmen are the road's reminder of what that glory costs.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகட்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hot track lined with the graves of travellers

comparisons.tenor: her hair, or her as its wearer

occasion.words: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகட்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது

232.reading: With the hero listening, the friend tells the girl that her bond with the lord of the rock country, where an elephant takes midnight thunder for a tiger and flees, has now brought on the season when mother, guarding the house, has the velan come, saying it is Murugu, with mixed flower offerings, in a courtyard strewn with vengai gold like a festival ground where the kuravar women dance.
232.nuance: The velan's rite shows the secret is close to discovery: the mother reads the girl's lovesickness as Murugu's seizure. The elephant mistaking thunder for a tiger matches the mother mistaking love for possession; we leave it as scene because only one correspondence holds firmly.

colophon.thurai: தோழி, தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்ச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai, the hill people and their kuravai dance

233.reading: The friend tells the weeping girl that though he has crossed a summer track of fire-blackened land where lean elephants languish and short and tall hills crowd together like the host of ghouls gathered at Uthiyan Cheral's great feast, he will not linger over wealth, forgetting the sweet sleep of her dark hair.
233.nuance: The Cheral's great feast, a puram fame, is turned into a picture of the landscape: the hills crowd like the ghoulish guests. The friend's assurance turns on the same memory of sleep in her hair that poem 223 uses.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகட்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: summer, and the track where the rain has gone

comparisons.tenor: the short and tall hills crowded together

234.reading: The hero tells his charioteer to drive the swan-swift horses fast over the rain-washed sand, so that by dusk, when the doe frolics with the stag and bees hum at the mullai, he may reach the pleasant woodland town where his pale, tear-eyed wife can at last undo her braid.
234.nuance: The braid is a sign: she bound her hair at his leaving and will loosen it at his return, so his speed is measured by her hair. The doe at play with the stag is what the arrival will be.

colophon.thurai: தலைமமகன் தேர்ப்பாகற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains, the evening and the mullai flower

iraicchi.act: the young doe, tired of browsing, frolics unharmed in the joy of joining the stag
iraicchi.sense: the wife's release at his return will be as glad and as safe as the doe's play with her mate

235.reading: The girl asks her friend whether, set on wealth, he has not thought of them, or thinking has forgotten for his greater work, while the cold north wind and the drizzling east cloud open the thonri like a lamp and the musundai like stars on the grass, the crab hides in its hole, and the graceless wind torments her at evening, he who never asked what would become of her, pale and wasted.
235.nuance: The season is the rains and the cold wind, and the torment is the evening: by the Tholkappiyam's times this is mullai waiting, though the colophon files the poem as paalai because he went for wealth.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகள் ஆற்றாமைமீதூரத் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a woman waits through the rains and suffers the evening; she is not on the road

comparisons.tenor: the white musundai flowers on the grass

236.reading: The girl tells her friend that, not knowing how great the town lord's love was, she suffered: last night, not knowing he lay among bejewelled women, she went about with a broken heart telling her trouble, like Aathi Manthi who lost her lover and asked land after land whether anyone had seen Attan Atthi, crying that the sea had taken him, the flood had hidden him.
236.nuance: The phrase about the greatness of his love is bitter: the love she did not know was his love for others. She casts herself as the tragic Manthi while he was safe among other women, and the gap between the legend and his conduct is the reproach.

colophon.thurai: ஆற்றாமை வாயிலாகப் புக்க தலைமகன் நீக்கத்துக்கண் புக்க தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband's night among other women and the wife's reproach

occasion.words: ஆற்றாமை வாயிலாகப் புக்க தலைமகன் நீக்கத்துக்கண் புக்க தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது

237.reading: The friend tells the girl to stop grieving that the spring nights, with paathiri flowers on the sand and the south wind in the kuravam, pass sleepless: even if he reached rich Uranthai, where roast meat, millet, cane syrup and milk-soaked rice flakes are shared out, he would not stay there for his work's sake, away from the sweetness of her mouth.
237.nuance: The friend answers spring with plenty: the feast-town of Uranthai is the strongest temptation she can name, and she sets the girl's mouth above it.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளைத் தோழி வற்புறீஇயது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is away on his work through the spring

occasion.words: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளைத் தோழி வற்புறீஇயது

238.reading: The friend asks the hill lord who has come by night, where a tiger rises at midnight to fetch food for his mate weak after bearing young, kills a bull gaur and drags it reddening the rock, whether, if he parts from her, he has any cure for her forehead, fragrant as the kaanthal on the slopes of Nalli, whose giving pours like rain.
238.nuance: Kapilar sets the tiger's care for his new mother against the hero's night visits: the beast provides, and the question is whether the man will. Nalli's generosity, praised in passing, gives the girl's fragrance a patron's fame.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறி வந்த தலைமகற்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: midnight on the hill slope

iraicchi.act: the tiger goes out at midnight to bring prey to his mate, weak and hungry after giving birth
iraicchi.sense: the man who comes by night should, like the tiger, take on the care of the woman rather than leave her

239.reading: Leaving for wealth, the hero tells his heart how pitiable is the fine town of the little girl who only yesterday, with long and short sulks and many sweet words, asked whether he would not stay long away, crossing rivers of strange lands on tracks where red-eyed raiders roaring like tigers seize cattle at night, while the women here worship the crescent at dusk.
239.nuance: Her question is quoted whole inside his speech, so the poem is her protest overheard in his memory. The cattle raid on the track is puram matter (vetchi) seen from the akam side, as a danger the girl names.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்துபோகாநின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is leaving for wealth

occasion.words: பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்துபோகாநின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

240.reading: The friend tells the man who came by night that the shore grove is no longer empty at night, for father goes out to the fishing lamps and mother worships at the haunted ford with her companions, so if he wants to sleep on the girl's breast he should come to the punnai grove in the white-sand nook where the seruthi blooms.
240.nuance: The stork flying over the backwater, mindful of its lone nestling, could carry a sense for a man who leaves a girl alone; we leave it as scene because the poem's own point is the household's night movements. Line 4's புலம்பின்றே can be read as 'not lonely' (crowded) or the reverse, and the advice turns on it.

colophon.thurai: தோழி, இரவுக்குறிவந்த தலைமகற்குப் பகற்குறி நேர்ந்தது.

thinai_evidence.note: the neythal flower, the punnai grove and the fishing boats

links.note: Both use the Kazhar legend of Aathi Manthi and Attan Atthi; 222 names Maruthi, who restored the lover and entered the sea, 236 has Manthi searching town after town.
links.teaches: One legend served two speakers: the friend holds up Maruthi's fatal deed as a fame to win, the wife holds up Manthi's lament as her own shame, so the story was a shared stock the poets bent to opposite purposes.

links.note: Both marutham poems reproach the husband for bathing in the Kaveri flood with the woman he desires (நீ வெய் யோளொடு), and both place it at Matthi's Kazhar near Thithan's Uranthai.
links.teaches: The shared phrase and places show that the bathing scandal at Kazhar was a set situation of marutham, which each poet then sharpened with a different puram comparison, a rout in 226 and a lost youth in 6.

links.note: Both measure gossip against a public spectacle: the Kural against the serpent swallowing the moon, the Akananuru against the shout at Katti's flight.
links.teaches: The Kural keeps the old akam habit of sizing a private scandal by a famous public event, but trades the historical rout for a cosmic eclipse, losing the political sting while keeping the scale.

links.note: Thazhumban's Unur stands as the measure of wealth in both, here as the region beyond which the lover's noisy departure is likened to Marungur's market, there as the town a girl's beauty is compared to.
links.teaches: A chieftain's town famous in puram praise was reused by akam poets as a ready scale of plenty, so a patron's fame circulated as a stock of comparison across the two kinds of poem.

links.note: Both set the absent man's wellbeing above the woman's pallor: the friend's blessing நோய்இலராக, the Kural's 'let my body pale, if he is well'.
links.teaches: The Kural compresses into the woman's own mouth a blessing that the Akananuru gives to the friend, showing how the anthology's go-between voice was absorbed into the single speaker of the later couplets.

links.note: Both refuse the promise of a quick return: the girl quotes his 'we will come right away' against the spring, the Kural says tell your quick return to those who will be alive.
links.teaches: Read together they show the same refusal of comfort in two registers, the Kural as a sharp retort before parting and the Akananuru as proof gathered afterwards from the season's signs.

links.note: In both the girl looks and bows her head; the Kural takes it as water poured into the bond, while here the bowed head with checked tears leaves the hero in pain.
links.teaches: The Kural fixes the bowed head as a sign of consent, but the Akananuru shows the same gesture as unreadable to the man at the moment it happens, so the maxim is a reading made after the fact.

links.note: Both give the man's reason for parting as the pursuit of glory or strength (நல்லிசை, உரன்), which takes his resolve as companion instead of her.
links.teaches: The friend's argument that glory is not for those who stay home is the very reason the Kural's woman lives on in longing, so the same heroic value comforts in one poem and wounds in the other.

links.note: Uthiyan Cheral's great feast (பெருஞ்சோறு) is praised in Purananuru 2 as a king's gift; here the crowd at that feast becomes a simile for hills crowding on the desert track.
links.teaches: An akam poet could assume his hearers knew a king's famous feast well enough to turn its crowd of eaters into a picture of a landscape, which tells us how far puram fame was common knowledge.

links.note: Both have the returning man wish to finish the work and reach home for the evening; the Kural's evening feast at home is the poem's dusk arrival when the wife loosens her braid.
links.teaches: The Kural states as a wish what the mullai poem stages as a drive at dusk, showing that the evening return was the fixed goal of the man's speech in both traditions.

links.note: In both the evening comes with cold and brings the woman's sorrow to its height.
links.teaches: The Kural names the evening's chill and the swelling grief in two lines, while the Akananuru supplies the season's things, the north wind, the rain and the flowers, that make the evening cold, so the couplet presupposes the landscape.

links.note: Both are the friend's assurance that he will return; 231 grants that glory took him away, 237 says no rich town, not even Uranthai, will keep him from her.
links.teaches: Taken together the two comforts answer the two fears of the waiting woman, that his honour will keep him away and that pleasure will, and show the friend's arguments as a set repertoire.

links.note: Both liken the woman's fragrance to the kaanthal flowers of Nalli's hill slopes.
links.teaches: Nalli's hill and its kaanthal were a fixed image for a woman's scent, so a patron's country lent its fame to the beloved's body in more than one poet's hands.

links.note: The Kural commands making wealth as the sharpest weapon; the hero leaving for wealth that is hard to earn counts what the going costs the girl he leaves.
links.teaches: The Kural's bare imperative to make wealth is weighed here against a girl's quoted plea not to stay long, showing that the duty the maxim states without condition was, in akam, always paid for by someone left behind.

new_concepts.gloss: marriage, as the friend presses the lover toward it to end the secret affair
new_concepts.label_source: ours: the tradition's term; the poems imply it without naming it

source_issues: akananuru:224: line 13 reads குரலிசைப் கடுப்ப; the doubled ப் before க is not regular sandhi and is probably a misprint for குரலிசை கடுப்ப.
akananuru:225: the flag reports 17 lines in our base text against 18 in the commentary edition (pmuni0523_02); the poem reads complete as it stands, but the lineation differs.
akananuru:230: lineation flag: a printed line number 5 stands on line 10 of the base text.
akananuru:234: the colophon thurai has தலைமமகன், a doubled ம, for தலைமகன்; copied as is in `colophon`.
akananuru:236: line 5 இடைனில is probably இடைநில, and line 10 உய்ர்த்தனென் is probably உயிர்த்தனென்.
akananuru:238: line 10 பெருகல் நாட is probably பெருங்கல் நாட, the usual epithet of the hill lord.
